Dynamic crystalline imperfections such as phase errors can significantly hinder the imaging and analysis capabilities of a transmission electron microscope. While traditional correctors like a programmable phase disk operate at low frequencies and correct static imperfections, their effectiveness in addressing dynamic errors is questionable due to the high speed at which these errors occur. This paper investigates the feasibility of using a programmable phase disk to compensate for dynamic crystalline imperfections and suggests an experimental setup to test this hypothesis. Furthermore, it explores alternative strategies for correcting dynamic errors, including a proposed method to correct errors occurring at a frequency comparable to the TEM's spin frequency.

The success of deep generative models heavily relies on their ability to capture complex data patterns through compact latent variables. In the case of conversational models, researchers have primarily focused on models that output next utterances based on past dialogue and generate internal states that represent user preferences. Although these models produce high-quality conversations, their generative processes are underutilized. In this research, we argue that both the dialogue and user preference should be encoded into a unified representation of user intent. To validate this argument, we experiment with a generative approach for RNN-based dialogue models that encodes both factors. Our results show that this approach enhances both conversation quality and the accuracy of predicted user responses.

This project introduces a novel, attention-driven deep learning location recognition network that utilizes 3D LiDAR data.  LiDAR data is crucial for vehicle positioning, but its processing is complicated due to varying levels of noise and a vast amount of data.  Our approach combines an upsampling module, a two-stage feature extraction module, and a classification module to tackle these challenges.  Specifically, our designed LiDAR sampling module reduces data size and removes noise, while our proposed dual attention-driven deep learning module effectively captures both local and global information from LiDAR data.  Experimental results show our method's superior performance compared to existing methods, achieving a location recognition accuracy of 98.5%.

Video transcoding is an intensive computing task that's often outsourced to cloud service providers. To reduce costs, cloud vendors utilize a mix of new and old hardware, creating a heterogeneous cloud environment. In this study, we evaluate the performance of transcoding videos across different types of heterogeneous cloud resources, specifically CPU-based and GPU-based machines running the H.264 standard. Our assessments were conducted on multiple cloud service providers, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure, using videos ranging from 720p to 1080p at 30 frames per second. Our findings show that while Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud Platform offer more affordable resource pricing, Microsoft Azure provides better performance due to its use of GPU-based resources. Our results also indicate that H.264 transcoding on Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud Platform can be significantly sped up through parallel processing. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the potential for optimizing transcoding performance in a heterogeneous cloud environment by selecting the most suitable type of resource for each task.

This work offers a new explanation for a previously observed anomaly in doped graphene panels near room temperature, known as the particular heat. We demonstrate that the unusual heat capacity can be attributed to the shielding of doped sites by undoped regions, a phenomenon that can be universally observed in doped semimetallic monolayers. Additionally, a theoretical model based on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model is developed to further understand this shielding effect and its impact on the specific heat of these panels.

Conditional text-to-speech generation aims to produce speech that conveys both audio content and text content, enabling more natural text-to-speech systems. Current models struggle with processing complex contexts, as they often process sparse information and ignore multi-faceted contextual relationships. To address this issue, we introduce MaskedSpeech, a novel approach that allows models to infer missing information by masking text conditions and learning from the data. MaskedSpeech employs a masking strategy, where the model infers the text that corresponds to the masked portions of the audio, given the full context. We incorporate this context-learning context into the generation process, resulting in a context-aware model. Experimental results show that MaskedSpeech outperforms existing models in terms of accuracy and naturalness.

This paper provides a comprehensive review of recent research on the discrete Klein-Gordon model. Various concepts and findings related to this model are explored, particularly concerning spectral and orbital stability. Key results are summarized, including those by Butusov, Grunert, and Séré, which demonstrate the existence of standing waves in the form of solutions that decay and occur at specific frequencies. Additionally, the existence of periodic solutions is proven for both monotone and non-monotone force functions, as well as the identification of minimal energy required for these solutions based on their period.

Q-ball models that incorporate multiple types of charge have been examined, and it has been determined that they can form large, compact structures akin to nuclei in addition to their typical diffuse Q-ball formations. Furthermore, the relationship between the multiple types of charge and the size of these compact entities can be easily described using a parametric equation.

We investigate the impact of a cyclic universe on the interplay between dark energy and holographic cosmology, specifically examining the influence of a finite universe size on the critical energy density cutoff. By adapting the initial condition of the dark energy density within a cyclic universe model, we explore how this influence affects different choices of the proportionality coefficient in the hypothesis. Our analysis reveals that, in contrast to a static universe scenario, the influence of the universe's size becomes negligible in cyclic universe models for a wide range of parameter values, and we also discuss the implications of our findings within this theoretical framework.
Given a Hermitian matrix whose structure follows a graph, this report investigates how its scattering matrix relates to the number of positive and negative eigenvalues.

We examine Leopoldt's conjecture through the lens of non-commutative algebraic number theory, focusing on the properties of p-adic Lie fields without a commutative counterpart. Our study derives fresh insights into the structure of the Iwasawa algebra within such an extension, directly proving the algebra's uniqueness and revealing its isomorphism to a power series ring over the integral p-adic numbers. We also establish the finiteness of the p-rank of the ideal class group within certain maximal abelian p-extension subfields.

We explore the connection between non-observation and discovery in particle physics, specifically in relation to future experiments at Belle II. As an illustration, we examine axial vector meson decays into two photons and consider vector and scalar mesons for comparison. The potential for axial vector meson discovery at Belle II is assessed, given that the KLOE experiment has already observed similar decays. The sensitivity of Belle II to rare decays like $B^+\to K^+ \mathcal{A}_1^+$ and $B_s\to \mathcal{A}_1$, which could indicate the presence of axion-like particles, is investigated.

Understanding changes in meaning across various domains is a significant challenge that linguistics and natural language processing are still grappling with. This paper proposes a contextualized language framework to guide the investigation into semantic alteration detection. This framework enables us to identify key factors that contribute to the detection of semantic alteration, including linguistic elements, contextual aspects, and knowledge representation. We then explore two contextualized language frameworks to gather data for evaluating semantic alteration detection, resulting in two new datasets: COWEN and COWEN_B. These frameworks and evaluation results provide a foundation for further research into the development of effective strategies for identifying semantic alteration.

The formation of supermassive black holes and their subsequent accretion disks can be influenced by the presence of ultralight bosons, particularly those with masses ranging from $10^{-12}$ eV to $10^{-6}$ eV. This could potentially be observed through the spin properties of massive quasar black holes. A significant correlation has been found between low-spin black holes and the presence of ultralight scalars, while massive quasar binaries with significant spin values suggest the existence of ultralight axions. Furthermore, a distinct pattern has been identified in the distribution of black hole masses, with a noticeable change occurring at $10^{7}$ solar masses. This change can be attributed to the growth of black holes through ultralight boson condensation and accretion, with larger black holes having more access to fuel for growth.

During retinal development, neuroblols undergo a specific phase where they stop cell cycle progression but remain within their nuclei. This study focuses on retinal development in zebrafish, analyzing the movement of nuclei during this specific period. Researchers observed the positions of retinal nuclei at various time points using confocal microscopy and tracked their movement. They found that the nuclei's displacement follows an exponential pattern, shifting from moving freely within the space to moving in a more confined manner. This change is influenced by the interaction between the nuclei and surrounding substances. A theoretical model was created to better understand the underlying forces at play. The study found that certain nuclei move in an elastic environment, while others move in a more open space. This has implications for understanding how retinal cells develop and may be applicable to other tissues as well.

We introduce an advanced approach to identifying source images within a collection of related images, which is a crucial step in various techniques for processing colored video. This method combines a collection of sophisticated algorithms, encompassing related images extraction, source segmentation, and related video reconstruction. To determine the optimal range of the structure preservation parameter, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the reconstructed images and employed a combination of visual inspection and automated evaluation techniques. This approach was successfully applied to a collection of real-world video clips, yielding satisfactory results.

This study numerically investigates active Brownian particles within two-dimensional obstacles using lattice models, specifically examining the system's behavior near corner regions where the geometry consists of two perpendicular walls. We compared this to particles in a single wall system and found that in the one-dimensional configuration, the system behaves like a standard active particle with modified diffusion. However, in the two-dimensional system with angles other than right angles, we observed anomalous diffusion with an effective dimension greater than two. This behavior is attributed to the formation of an excluded volume due to the disorder, which significantly impacts the system's dynamics. Our simulations indicate that this effect is most pronounced in right-angle corners, leading to an effective dimension close to three. These findings provide valuable insights into the complex interplay between active matter and geometric constraints.

Academic cooperation networks are intricate structures that encompass a wide range of relationships and intricate patterns. As the structures of scholarly cooperation networks are dynamic in nature, they are subject to continuous changes over time. To comprehensively analyze the underlying structures of these networks, it is essential to consider their temporal aspects. To achieve this, we propose a new evaluation metric, the network structure change rate, which quantifies the rate of structural change within a time interval. This metric is designed to identify communities within the network by pinpointing nodes with high structure change rates. To validate the effectiveness of this metric, we applied it to analyze the underlying structures of the CS (Computer Science) cooperation network over time. The results obtained from this analysis were compared with the community structures identified using the Louvain algorithm, demonstrating a high degree of similarity. Furthermore, the results also revealed that certain disciplines, such as Computer Vision and Image Processing, are prone to fluctuations in their cooperation structures.

Copper-based compounds with a pyrochlore structure display a unique pseudogap state around the vertical axis of the Fermi surface, characterized by the d-orbital of copper.  This research reveals that substituting copper with nickel in these materials creates new states near the vertical axis of the Fermi surface, resulting in a weak pseudogap state.  Using resonant photoemission spectroscopy and theoretical calculations, we found that these states are due to an overlap between the lower Hubbard band and a ligand band, leading to a charge-transfer pseudogap.  This research highlights the distinction between this type of pseudogap and those caused by strong electron-electron interactions.

A novel device has been created to detect spallation neutrons produced in Aberdeen Tunnel's 10MeV spallation facility. The device utilizes a 10-inch thick Cadmium block, which effectively absorbs incident protons and emits a stream of neutrons. To amplify the weak neutron signal, a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) is positioned opposite the Cadmium block's face. The SiPM's readings can be further validated by using a silicon detector to observe the remaining protons. The device's performance has been demonstrated through the use of both natural and artificial neutron sources, as well as the spallation neutrons. It has been found that a specific type of source, the Cadmium-proton source, can offer a comparable level of sensitivity to conventional neutron flux measurements.

This paper investigates a nonlocal biharmonic Choquard equation of the form
$$
\begin{cases}
\Delta^2u-\lambda\Delta u= \lambda u+ (u\cdot T_\lambda f(u))\cdot f(u) & x\in\mathbb{R}^4,\\
u\in H^{4,2}(\mathbb{R}^4) & x\in\mathbb{R}^4.
\end{cases}
$$
The primary objective is to find ground state solutions for this problem where the function $f(u)$ exhibits exponential critical growth and $T_\lambda f(u)$ has power-type decay. A variational approach combined with the concentration compactness principle enables the proof of existence for a ground state solution, considering specific assumptions on $\lambda$ and $f$. Notably, this study overcomes the challenges posed by the lack of compactness resulting from the combined critical exponential growth and decay behavior.

The TESS mission has significantly expanded our knowledge of the sky by systematically searching for transiting exoplanets, complementing previous findings and accelerating the discovery of planetary systems. TESS has also identified numerous astrophysical phenomena, such as variable stars and stellar activity, which can be studied to gain insights into the properties of stars. To study the habitability of exoplanets, particularly those orbiting within the TESS photic zone, accurate knowledge of host star properties and activity is crucial. The TESS-Keck Assessment aims to determine the most scientifically valuable targets for follow-up observations, taking into account the needs of both exoplanet research and stellar astronomy. A hierarchical framework is proposed to prioritize targets based on their astrophysical significance, considering factors such as detection confidence, research potential, and data availability. A weighted scoring system is introduced to rank targets according to their habitability potential, allowing for a comprehensive assessment of the TESS sample. The results of the assessment show that a diverse range of targets are selected, including small stars with multiple planets, which are of particular interest for future research. The outcomes of the assessment can be applied to the selection of targets for upcoming missions such as the TESS Continuous Survey and the TESS Science Archive.

This research focuses on developing an ID document extractor for the Indonesian people's empowerment center, utilizing Character Recognition and Language Processing to facilitate access to essential information about Indonesian citizens. An accurate ID verification system is crucial for preventing identity fraud and enhancing the reliability of data obtained from the ID. This project employs a deep learning-based ID recognition method, specifically the TensorFlow framework, to extract and interpret the information contained within the Indonesian ID card. The study successfully demonstrates precise ID card extraction and interpretation, utilizing a combination of Character Recognition and Language Processing to facilitate access to essential information about Indonesian citizens.

A new Monte Carlo simulation method for calculating the propagation of a quantum harmonic oscillator in one dimension has been developed, incorporating initial positions and momenta at the start of the process. This approach is based on molecular path integral theory and utilizes positions of the particle for data analysis. Unlike traditional methods, it does not require knowledge of the particle's momentum during the process. A key feature of our method is its ability to accommodate systems with external forces and friction, resulting in shifted equilibrium positions and altered oscillation frequencies. A simulation system has been created and demonstrated, consisting of a quantum particle in a one-dimensional trap within a damped harmonic oscillator setup.

We analyzed three asteroids, 1992 SK, Toro, and Geographos, using light curve data from previous studies along with rotational dynamics simulations to determine their rotation speed changes caused by the YORP effect. By combining these light curve periods with their respective mass estimates, we calculated the YORP effect's torque for each asteroid. The results show that 1992 SK and Geographos are experiencing a spin-up effect, while Toro is spin-down. Furthermore, 1992 SK and Geographos are not close to reaching rotational failure, as indicated by their F values, while Toro is approaching this threshold. By predicting their rotation speeds in 10,000 years, we found that 1992 SK and Geographos will maintain their current rotation patterns, while Toro may enter a period of rapid acceleration before potentially experiencing rotational failure.

Social media platforms have become a key means of communication and information dissemination, with users engaging in a wide range of topics from politics to entertainment. These platforms serve as a vital source of information that reflects societal values and beliefs, offering valuable insights into the collective mindset of a society. In this study, we employ network science to analyze the dynamics of political discussions on Instagram, focusing on the connections between users and their interactions within the network. By examining the subgroups, user activity, and the spread of information within the network, we can better understand the complex relationships between individuals and the spread of political ideas. Furthermore, by integrating linguistic analysis with network science, we can gain a more comprehensive view of the underlying structure of these conversations and the diverse range of opinions expressed. Ultimately, our research highlights the potential of using social networks to track public opinion and the spread of political ideas, which can inform policy decisions and promote democratic engagement.

We demonstrate that any compact collection of homeomorphisms mapping the unit disk to itself, which preserves the center, will also be compact when homeomorphisms that do not lead to boundary point divergence are considered. Furthermore, the previous proof by Beardon and Minda, which relied on the modular capacity, is modified to a more intuitive approach. The necessity of restricting the divergence at the boundary is demonstrated through the non-compactness of Cole's rotation collection, which consists of homeomorphisms of the form $f(re^{it}) = (r^3\cos(t), r^3\sin(t))$ and $R_\alpha \circ f \circ R_{-\alpha}$, where $R_\alpha$ denotes a rotation by angle $\alpha$.

Low-mass stars offer valuable opportunities for studying stellar activity and the habitability of their planetary systems. However, the lack of comprehensive spectral databases for these stars hinders such research. To address this issue, we present a new collection of 130 high-quality M-dwarf spectra spanning a wide range of spectral types. These M1.0 to M7.0 stars were observed using the IUE, providing a robust set of data for researchers. Our analysis of these spectra reveals that our collection is diverse, encompassing stars with varying ages, metallicities, and levels of activity. Notably, our study shows that the new M-dwarf spectra are distinct from the typical one-dex breadth of available public spectra, and we demonstrate their potential for accurately determining the physical properties of exoplanets. Additionally, our findings suggest that these high-quality spectra can be used to study the abundance patterns of M-dwarf stars and their habitability.

Two-dimensional photonic crystals can trap and guide edge states along interfaces, 
offering potential for on-chip light manipulation. 
However, these states have limitations due to their inability to be controlled. 
This study proposes a novel solution by introducing a specific dual interface 
between specially designed photonic crystals. 
It is found that a specific orientation of a unit cell can prevent backscattering 
of light, whereas other orientations result in state localization. 
Interestingly, this dual localization effect can be utilized to guide line states, 
and by adjusting the interface, state localization can be achieved even without 
trapped modes. 
Furthermore, this design demonstrates robustness against structural imperfections 
and demonstrates the ability to guide states in both directions. 
By applying this concept to photonic applications, highly localized states with 
large field confinement and low propagation loss can be created.

We examine how certain modifications to standard relational database queries impact their processability, specifically looking at self-joint queries and inverse query disjunctions. We provide ranking systems for both types of queries based on difficulty, then break down the complexity of evaluating them in various scenarios. Our analysis reveals the underlying logical structures responsible for complexity differences, enabling us to identify key parameters that influence query evaluation efficiency. We also design optimized algorithms for specific query forms and explore their performance characteristics in detail.

Karp's concept of infinite sequence functions was a significant achievement in the realm of theoretical computer science. However, it lacked practical utility due to its limited focus on non-deterministic computation. To address this shortcoming, a new approach has been proposed that leverages stream processing frameworks to provide an efficient computational model for infinite sequence functions. This approach utilizes a structured language based on Datalog with negation and fixed point, and establishes its theoretical properties. The proposed approach is further validated through the development of a stream processing framework, which demonstrates the feasibility of the computational model. The framework's capabilities are showcased through the implementation of complex data analysis algorithms, including anomaly detection and natural language processing techniques.

Employing a MNLO effective Hamiltonian along with form factors from the Bourrely-Cohen-Legrand model, this study analyzes $B^0 \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ and $B^+ \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ decays, enabling the extraction of specific B-meson decay constants and triplet-pole angles. Additionally, it estimates the $B^0 \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ branching ratio, obtaining $0.14 \times 10^{-6}$ at an confidence interval of $68\%$.

In the context of swarms, swarms exhibit multiple coexisting behaviors that balance between stability and adaptability. To achieve this balance, we present a novel neural network design, the learning hidden coexisting swarms (LHCS), which utilizes swing networks and switch networks to manage different behavioral states. Swing networks enable the swarm to transition between states, while switch networks allow for the selection of the appropriate network to engage. We have demonstrated that this system can effectively respond to changes in the environment and maintain a balance between stability and adaptability.

This study focuses on determining the average absolute deviation from the midpoint of a random variable X, and it involves the development of two bias-corrected estimators for this parameter. Specifically, the study introduces an unbiased bias-reduced estimator by leveraging the concept of combinatorial identities. In addition, the performance of this bias-reduced estimator is compared to other methods, including the maximum likelihood and median estimators. Furthermore, the study provides a Monte Carlo simulation to assess the performance of the proposed bias-reduced estimator.

A novel approach is proposed for approximating reachable sets of nonlinear control systems subject to constraints, by leveraging a modified Variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation of Cauchy type. This approach is unique in its consideration of curvature effects, which are often overlooked in traditional methods. We provide theoretical justification for our method and support it through numerical implementation, which includes a way to solve the complex Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the refinability of our solution, which ensures the accuracy of the reachable set approximation. A carefully designed numerical scheme is proposed for the calculation of the modified equation, which is robust in the presence of discontinuities. This scheme is further enhanced by a technique for reducing the number of subgradients to be evaluated. Additional methods for reducing the dimensionality of the problem are proposed, which include a technique for exploiting system symmetries. Our method is shown to outperform state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency.

We introduce a novel class of dynamic, modulated cyclic activations in hidden units, which effectively capture long-term dependencies and facilitate the representation of complex, hierarchical structures. This innovative approach enables neural networks to efficiently represent complex patterns and structures, even when they operate in silico. Notably, our method overcomes the limitations of traditional modulated cyclic activations, providing a robust solution for the exact computation problem. We demonstrate that our solution outperforms recent advances in neural network performance, achieving a significant leap in accuracy and reliability.

The brain's exceptional ability to process information is thought to be due to pre-established neural connections that facilitate complex computations. Recent research has revealed a pattern in the arrangement of stimuli that influence ventral temporal cortex, specifically its association with the categorization of living and non-living things. However, the animacy effect's presence in ventral temporal cortex was previously unclear. In this study, we used a combination of intracranal electroencephalogram and functional magnetic resonance imaging to investigate the animacy effect's presence in participants' brains. Our findings show a clear arrangement of living and non-living stimuli in the temporal lobe, which is not a result of physical differences in the stimuli but rather reflects the functional organization of the brain. This discovery sheds light on the neural mechanisms behind object recognition and categorization.

This research establishes the quantum unique ergodicity (QUE) property for form factor correlations at any positive depth $T$ with a power saving uniformity for the Hecke-Maass newforms in $[0,<\frac{n}{4}-\frac{3}{8})$. As a consequence, we obtain the non-vanishing of Hecke-Lambda zero-free regions near the critical strip for a substantial proportion of primitive Dirichlet characters $\chi$ specifically, we show that there exists some constant $\delta > 0$ where the number of such characters modulo $q$ can be lower-bounded by $\phi(q)/q^{1-\delta}$.

We have developed a quantum relational Hoare logic that builds upon the existing classical framework, extending it to incorporate expectations and assigning variables, and done so by expanding a previously quantified sumability requirement for safety. This condition ensures that the act measures being summed do not exceed the maximum possible value of one. Our logic enables proving the validity of safety, expectation properties, and concurrent behaviors, and can also be utilized to develop quantitative invariants for concurrent acts through a set of rules. These invariants can be relational and can include values greater than one, and we have demonstrated their effectiveness using a set of examples that include the Fork-Join act, and we have developed an abstract interpretation framework to automatically verify safety, expectations, and relational invariants for quantum programs. This interpretation framework uses a non-interfering abstract domain and we have demonstrated its correctness and precision using a set of test cases.

The rapid transmission of a contagious disease often involves a small number of individuals who infect a large number of other people, known as super-spreaders. Due to their significant role in the spread of an epidemic, understanding and identifying super-spreaders is crucial for effective intervention. A common approach to modeling the early stages of an epidemic is using a branching process, which can be adapted to incorporate varying transmission rates among individuals, referred to as a heterogeneous Galton-Watson process. In this context, we examine the characteristics of super-spreaders and the impact of their actions on the overall development of an epidemic. Our research reveals that, during the initial stages of an outbreak, most individuals who contribute to its spread are among those who have infected the most people, and it can lead to its rapid decline when a certain number of individuals fail to transmit the disease. Moreover, our theoretical analysis and numerical simulations demonstrate that, in order for a certain threshold to be reached, only a small proportion of the population needs to be infected. Ultimately, this proportion is influenced by the degree of heterogeneity in transmission rates, and it can be interpreted as a critical point in determining the outcome of an epidemic.

Building upon the concepts of codiskcyclicity, this investigation extends the framework to include Reflexive Topological Algebraic Convex Conical Linear Ordered (R.T.A.C.C.L.L.) spaces and locally solid R.T.A.C.C.L.L. spaces. As a consequence, we derive codiskcyclicity criteria for operator collections defined on these specialized spaces. Subsequently, we examine hypercyclicity in operator collections defined on certain Topological Vector Spaces (T.V.S.s), with the focus particularly on nilpotent operator collections within these spaces.

Vector magnetograms are crucial for understanding solar phenomena and space weather, but their reliability is compromised by non-thermal intensity information. Current methods struggle to accurately estimate the vector magnetic field from these imperfect data, and existing approaches have limitations in processing all three components of the magnetic field. This study presents two innovative techniques, one based on matrix inversion and the other on a modified Stenflo approximation, to derive more reliable vector magnetic fields. The results indicate that the new methods outperform existing models and offer improved resistance to bias. However, computational efficiency remains a challenge for the inverse method, prompting further investigation into optimizing the algorithm.

Researchers have utilized Gaia DR2 data to investigate the spatial dimensions of 21 young stellar clusters and associations located in the Milky Way, Andromeda, and Triangulum galaxies. By examining 20 in the Milky Way, one in Andromeda, and three in the Triangulum galaxy, we measured their radii across two dimensions and found that most are confined to the disk of their host galaxy. However, the stellar groups in the outer regions of the Milky Way demonstrate greater dispersion perpendicular to the galactic plane compared to those in the inner regions. This phenomenon may be a result of the spiral arms influencing the distribution of stars. Furthermore, we observed that the level of randomness in the stellar distribution increases with distance from the galactic center.

To enhance the precision of the Higgs boson search, we are working to improve measurements of heavy quarkonium states, specifically the charm quark pair states. In order to reduce systematic errors in these measurements, lattice QCD can provide exact values for certain decay widths, such as the two-photon decay of the $\eta_c$ meson. We have obtained a lattice QCD calculation of the $\eta_c \rightarrow \gamma \gamma$ decay width, which yields a value of 5.12 GeV$^{-2}$ for the amplitude $F_{\eta_c}$, based on a recent two-color spin-flip sum rule. By applying a perturbative correction, we derive a $\eta_c$ decay width of 3.38 $\pm$ 0.15 (stat) $\pm$ 0.16 (sys) keV, taking into account lattice and lattice-discretization uncertainties.

The Hubbard sign dilemma is a well-known obstacle in Monte Carlo simulations of fermionic systems, particularly when applied to larger systems or those with negative Hubbard U values. Due to the exponential increase in the number of sign changes with the system's size, traditional Monte Carlo methods become computationally unfeasible. In this study, we have discovered that by shifting to complex-valued wave functions, the Hubbard sign dilemma can be circumvented using a single computational algorithm. A novel, compact, complex-valued neural network is proposed, which has been found to accurately model ground and low-lying excited states in the single-band Hubbard model across the entire parameter range. Our approach has been shown to deliver highly precise results in terms of energies, occupations, and correlation functions, with remarkable computational efficiency.

Ehrlich previously proposed two conjectures regarding the Dickman $\rho$ function, specifically that there exists an integer threshold $N_0$ such that for all $n \ge N_0$, $\lfloor \rho(n) \rfloor = \lfloor \rho(N_0) \rfloor$ and that the equality $\lfloor \rho(n) \rfloor = \lfloor \rho(N_0) \rfloor$ holds for infinitely many values of $n$. In this study, we disprove Ehrlich's first conjecture by identifying a counterexample to Ehrlich's first equality, and demonstrating that the proposed equality is valid only for specific values of $n$ that can be expressed as $N_0 + k \cdot (N_0 - N_0)$, where $k$ is any non-negative integer and $N_0$ is the integer from the counterexample to Ehrlich's first conjecture.

This paper investigates the topological entropy and factor complexity of infinite words within the framework of semigroup theory. We establish a formula for the topological entropy of a word based on its factor complexity, and subsequently, we analyze how topological entropy and factor complexity interact with specific mappings on finite alphabets and free groups. These interactions lead to new results on the preservation of these properties under such transformations. Additionally, we derive a connection between the topological entropy of words and the asymptotic behavior of their subword recurrence coefficients.

Although creating advanced models that generalize across tasks has been extensively studied, the topic of enhancing models to adapt to new, unseen tasks without human feedback remains under-explored. In this study, we tackle the challenge of enabling pre-trained language models to successfully perform unrelated tasks without human feedback. Specifically, we focus on enabling models trained on sentence classification tasks to adapt to sentence-level factual questions. To achieve this, we propose a method that leverages an unsupervised retrieval enhancement technique to improve the models' ability to adapt to the target task. Our findings demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms baseline approaches on two different datasets.

This paper introduces a rapid, autonomous method for identifying and
segmenting objects in video using a lightweight framework called M-ar-K-Fast.
It builds upon the autonomous Stochastic Gradient descent principle,
integrating the M-ar-K-Fast object segmentation technique. Experiments conducted
on the P4D dataset demonstrate the method's effectiveness, with results showing
significant improvements in processing speed and reasonable accuracy levels.

The demand for video games has skyrocketed in recent years, fueling intense competition among developers. To gain a competitive edge, companies are increasingly focusing on the requirements phase of the software development lifecycle. However, traditionally, other development stages have been prioritized, often neglecting requirements analysis. This study delves into requirements engineering methodologies tailored for the video game industry, examining their theoretical underpinnings and practical applications through a systematic review. By doing so, it aims to establish requirements analysis as a crucial component of software development in the video gaming sector.

This paper proposes a hyperparameter tuning framework for neural networks that meet the requirements of differential privacy. We developed and tested this framework in conjunction with a secure image recognition network based on AlexNet. The results indicate that the proposed method optimally adjusts multiple parameters, including network hyperparameters and difference sensitivity, when privacy protections are implemented. The efficient and optimal hyperparameter tuning method developed enables the development of secure neural networks with reduced differential privacy costs.

A research focus known as Boolean structures arises when the properties of elements in an algebra can be deduced through a specific combination of element operations resulting in truth values. The study of Boolean structures in algebras of functions frequently centers on identifying sets of variables whose operations provide a truth-value basis. The research presented here delves into the Boolean structures of the algebra of functions mapping a set to itself, specifically those functions that remain unchanged when the set is reordered. The key findings demonstrate that any set of functions that provides a truth-value basis for the algebra of symmetric involutions must contain a sub-set of functions that does the same for a portion of the set, and that any set of functions that does the same for a set of odd cardinality includes one that does the same for a set of even cardinality. The study also determines the sets of essential functions that provide a truth-value basis for several subclasses of closed sets of functions.
