Unusually, eye-in-hand cameras do not require calibration, as their parameters are readily obtainable from images captured with known transformations. However, when camera parameters deviate over time due to mechanical wear, the ability to accurately identify objects from those images is compromised. Although the precise cause of this parameter drift is often unclear, the goal of this study is to establish an efficient eye-in-hand camera re-calibration method that utilizes only a single image from an object of known size. The method proposed involves the optimization of camera parameters to maximize the fit between the object's contour in the image and a 3D contour that rotates around the object's axis. The method is also enhanced to account for unknown object orientation and, ultimately, allows the calibration of all nine degrees of freedom from a single image. The proposed method is demonstrated through simulations and real-world experiments.

When addressing inverse problems, our objective is to reconstruct an original image from derived data generated by a known, linear operator. However, due to the inherent non-uniqueness of the problem, there can be multiple original images that result in the same data when processed by the operator. A prime example of an intricate application is phase retrieval, where a dominant technique utilizes measurements obtained from the intensity of the output. A primary issue with this approach lies in its inability to accurately reconstruct complex images from these measurements. A promising solution involves utilizing a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) to learn the reverse process by starting with noisy data and progressively generating a clear original image. To achieve this, we propose a novel training method that incorporates a regularization term, which encourages the data generated by the network to adhere to the underlying distribution of the original images.

This article investigates the behavior of invariant surfaces in dynamical systems that evolve according to a fractional order. We provide a general condition for invariant surfaces in such systems and illustrate our finding with various examples. This research extends previous studies on invariant structures in polynomial and semi-algebraic dynamical systems.

Next-generation wireless communication, specifically Terahertz transmissions, is set to overcome 5G's bandwidth limitations by utilizing the Terahertz frequency spectrum. To mitigate high path loss in the Terahertz spectrum, a multi-hop transmission approach is utilized, where shorter 5G transmission hops are linked via a Terahertz channel. Nevertheless, beam training in this frequency spectrum poses a significant challenge due to limited feedback resources. This paper introduces a novel reinforcement learning-based algorithm that dynamically optimizes the number of Terahertz hops, thereby enhancing the efficiency of the transmission. In simulated scenarios, this algorithm is shown to reduce beam training overhead by approximately 75% while maintaining acceptable communication link performance.

Pulsar scintillation allows for the study of the diffuse interstellar plasma that causes the intensity fluctuations of distant radio sources. By monitoring the scintillation of the bright pulsar B1133+16, we have created detailed maps of the electron density in the galaxy's interstellar medium within the line of sight to the LMC. Our findings reveal significant variations in scintillation patterns across different regions of the LMC, with some areas showing a notable increase in electron density, which may be indicative of a dense interstellar medium that could affect future radio observations in those regions.

To enhance music transcription accuracy, deep learning-based methods rely heavily on the quality of synthetic waveforms generated by models. However, existing neural networks produce waveforms of limited length and poor quality due to their reliance on autoregressive generation. In this research, a new framework called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet is proposed to overcome these limitations. This novel approach combines the speed and flexibility of an autoregressive model with a deep generative model, enabling the generation of high-quality waveforms over unlimited time spans. By leveraging a probabilistic model and a pitch-sensitive dilated convolutional neural network, Quasi-Periodic WaveNet learns to generate short segments of waveforms that accurately capture the complex signal characteristics of speech and music. Evaluation results demonstrate the superior performance of this model in terms of generation speed, quality, and spectral and perceptual metrics.

Arabic is a widely spoken language with significant historical importance and a large native speaker population. However, the lack of annotated natural language resources hampers the development of high-quality NLP applications for Arabic. While some open web platforms exist for basic text annotation, they are limited in scope and do not support the complex, collaborative annotation processes necessary for creating high-quality annotated datasets. MADARi, a new web platform, fills this gap by providing an environment for text annotation, specifically for morphological analysis in Arabic. It features a range of annotation tools and supports collaborative annotation, allowing annotators to review and amend previous notes. Additionally, the platform supports multiple user accounts, data management, and the integration of the spaCy NLP tool for automated annotation.

This study presents a photochemical analysis of temperate, low-density exoplanets, utilizing K-band spectral data to determine planetary temperatures.  We have developed a comprehensive model that accounts for radiative-thermal interactions, chemical reactions, and spectral observations.  The model is applied to analyze the atmospheric temperatures and compositions of these planets, with a focus on estimating the abundance of molecular species such as CO2, CO, CH4, and H2O.  The accuracy of the model is validated through comparison with 1D atmospheric models.  The results are discussed in the context of spectral data from the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope.  An appendix provides the rate coefficients for relevant chemical reactions.

To confirm the topological origin of the Majorana zero mode (MZM) peak in tunneling spectroscopy, we propose using dissipation as a distinguishing factor. We develop a model that incorporates a constant dissipation into the tunneling Hamiltonian and derive the conductance within the Malcher-Kastner approach. According to our theory, the peak associated with MZM exhibits a dissipation-independent conductance of 4e^2/h at zero bias, whereas other peaks' conductance increases linearly with dissipation strength. This difference in behavior can be experimentally observed through tunneling spectroscopy. We further demonstrate that a model with zero dissipation yields 4e^2/h conductance for the MZM peak, which contradicts previous studies.

As urbanization increases, road defects are becoming more prevalent and pose significant risks to road users. While numerous research areas have focused on identifying road issues, there is a lack of comprehensive studies that address the management of infrastructure assets. To bridge this gap, we developed a novel research framework and a corresponding system called RoadAtlas, which leverages advanced technologies to automate the process of road flaw detection and asset administration. By integrating these technologies, RoadAtlas streamlines the data collection, processing, and management stages, ultimately providing a comprehensive solution for the identification and management of road issues.

This paper introduces a bicategorical framework for shadows, comprising an idiomatic transformation functor from weighted comonads to the category of functors from the free monad on the underlying endofunctor to Comonads, which preserves certain structural characteristics. Additionally, we demonstrate that shadows are invariant under equivalence functors, demonstrating that they constitute an essential bicategorical marker.

We've developed a novel approach to audio localization that bypasses the need for pre-trained neural networks, which are typically relied upon in existing methods. Our approach is particularly useful in situations where only a limited number of source positions are available for training, or when source localization must be achieved using a very small dataset. By utilizing a set of training data consisting of recordings from multiple microphones and speakers, our method creates a set of virtual sensors and learns direct mappings between the actual sound sources and these virtual sensors. By leveraging simple set operations, our network can identify all possible source positions that could explain a particular set of audio data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by successfully localizing sounds in a large room with as few as 10 training samples, achieving accurate results by minimizing the number of possible source candidates.

This paper introduces the concept of Lorentzian Graph Neural Networks as a novel extension to existing Graph Neural Networks, adapting their structure to accommodate directed graphs with asymmetric edge relationships. By modifying the use of the aggregation function, we enable LorezGNNs to effectively process and interpret the significance of individual edges within a graph structure. We demonstrate the versatility of our model through successful applications in node classification and graph embedding tasks using publicly available benchmark datasets.

The primary objective of this research is to pinpoint the location of a vibrational structure embedded within a fluid using measurements of the surrounding fluid's movement. Consider a structure, such as a ship's hull, that is interacting with its surrounding environment and causing it to vibrate. Our goal is to determine the position of the structure based on the resulting fluid flow. This study focuses on the basic scenario where the structure's movement is not random but follows a cyclic, non-overlapping path. To solve this problem, we develop a method that uses time-reversal of the governing equations and a technique known as the adjoint state. This approach differs from traditional methods due to the lack of information about the structure's physical properties and the nature of its movement. The success of the algorithm is tested through the use of accurately created data and a straightforward implementation method. The results show that the method is effective in recovering the position of the structure under certain conditions, but its performance is limited by the structure's size and the frequency of its movement. The results also show that the method is robust to the presence of numerical errors and the use of a lower resolution grid. The study also highlights the need for further investigation into the use of the method in the presence of unknown boundary conditions and the use of the method in a real-world setting. A key objective in quantum-enhanced optical measurements is to maintain a squeezed state of an optomechanical system in a stable equilibrium. Achieving this goal has been hindered due to the absence of sufficient control over optomechanical systems. Our research introduces a novel approach using quantum feedback to control these systems, enabling us to create and sustain optical and optomechanical states that are squeezed. By designing a linear feedback controller based on measurements of the optomechanical system, we can establish stable equilibrium states that are optimized for squeezing through adjustment of the controller's parameters. Our theoretical model utilizes a framework of control theory to address this challenge and our optimization approach allows us to identify the optimal parameters for the feedback controller. Our approach is demonstrated to be effective through a range of scenarios, including various optomechanical configurations and levels of optical detuning. Our research provides a crucial step towards the advancement of quantum-enhanced optical measurements using controlled optomechanical systems.

We examine the fundamental characteristics of the classical scalar and vectorial mu-calculus in contrast to their extended versions that incorporate point designators. The enhanced versions enable a heightened descriptive capability over directed transition systems when dealing with both non-unary and unary operators. This enhancement can be achieved through a conversion technique, which transforms formulas with a basic set of operators into more complex forms with additional 'atomic' verification requirements, which, when combined with the designators, maintain their original properties. This approach serves as a basis for understanding the characteristics of the backward-looking Calcide mu-calculus.

A novel approach called the Exponential Delay Devaluation (Eddle) model has been introduced, which incorporates the concept of the power law, and it is argued that the Tsaitsis law, and specifically the Eddle law, can be viewed as an advanced, conceptually unified variation of both. The introduction of the devaluation factor and its associated devaluation index are key components of this model. Theoretical implications of the devaluation factor and index are explored, and their relevance to the devaluation of lag, as well as the concept of the Eddle factor, devaluation index, and the associated power law law, is discussed. The Eddle law, and its relationship to the power law law, can be applied to the analysis of the aging process, and in the context of the Eddle model, the probability density function, hazard function, mean residual life function, and reversed failure rate function can be determined, and their relationship to the devaluation factor and index can be explored. Considering the implications of heavy gravity in estimating average quantities,
we've re-evaluated the concept of the center of mass under such conditions,
and found that the traditional definition no longer holds. The modification
introduces a new type of 'harmonic' center that aligns with the laws of heavy
gravity, and for which a corresponding 'harmonic' mass gauge exists. This new
harmonic mass gauge exhibits properties analogous to those of the ordinary mass
gauge under normal gravity, and we've demonstrated this through various
calculations. The introduction of multiple centers and associated mass gauges
under heavy gravity is also discussed in our analysis.

A signed graph consists of a regular graph with edges that are either assigned a positive or negative sign. We can map a signed graph to another if the structure and signs of the edges are preserved. Recent research has heavily relied on expansions of unsigned graphs to determine chromatic numbers, but this approach has limitations. For some graphs, the chromatic number with respect to signed graphs is infinite. To address this issue, we propose expanded doubles as a new framework that accommodates both types of edges. By restricting the combination of edge types at adjacent edges in the expanded double model, we can better understand the chromatic behavior of large subsets of signed graphs. Using a tool called the regularity method, we can analyze the homomorphism density of these graphs and establish a theorem about their behavior. This allows us to derive thickness-based bounds for the chromatic number with respect to expanded graphs, providing a more effective representation for graph coloring problems.

The conventional method for identifying canonical equilibrium states relies on the condition that the average volume of phase space occupied by a system remains constant. An alternative criterion, based on the preservation of entropy, has also been proposed. In this study, we utilize Weyl-Wigner theory to demonstrate that these two approaches yield the same result when the system's fluctuations are taken into account. Notably, the constancy of entropy precisely equates to the constancy of the average volume of phase space, thereby confirming the initial assumption.

The concept of negative absolute temperature has historically been viewed with skepticism in the thermodynamics community, largely due to its initial discovery being limited to specific systems such as spin ensembles that decoupled from their surroundings. These circumstances led many to believe negative temperatures were a theoretical oddity with no practical significance. However, a recent breakthrough has challenged this perspective by demonstrating that negative absolute temperature can be attained for photons within a broader range of systems under certain conditions. This finding suggests that negative temperature is not as enigmatic or exclusive as previously thought, prompting calls for the thermodynamics community to reevaluate its understanding of this phenomenon.

This research paper builds upon recent developments in the theory of constrained sumsets of integers.
We establish a key property of bounded signed sumsets, which enables us to derive a straightforward result about their growth pattern and apply it to uncover insights regarding their structure.
Additionally, we obtain both direct and indirect consequences of a specific identity, related to the equal-weight case of Galperin's theorem, on bounded signed sumsets.
These outcomes allow us to determine the exact size of certain constrained sumsets, related to intervals, and related cyclic sumsets.

UniToPatho is a comprehensive dataset comprising 10,518 histopathological images, which are annotated at the slide level and contain 29,154 labels for objects within the images. This extensive collection is specifically designed to support the development of tasks related to colorectal polyp detection and analysis, including identifying and locating key features within the images. These features encompass polyp boundaries, tumor regions, and adenoma nuclei. Furthermore, the images are accompanied by corresponding reports, which are crucial for histological report generation and classification. Historically, pathologists have relied on classifying images based on report information, which has been done using both traditional and advanced methods. This extensive collection is being made available to facilitate the design of multimodal approaches that integrate visual and textual data, specifically for tasks such as image classification and report generation.

For long-wavelength diffusion scenarios with oscillating source terms, conventional methods like the finite element method face numerical instability. A new numerical approach is proposed, adapting the element size in the final term to source term frequency while adjusting the element size in the main term to ensure desired solution accuracy. This flexible element sizing can be seen as an extension of the piecewise linear method developed by Bastian and Knobbe, and high accuracy and stability are maintained for source terms with varying frequencies.

The proposed mechanism of a hydrothermal planetesimal accumulation explains the water found in chondrites by considering the composition of water and its delivery to early Earth. 
To demonstrate this mechanism, we used a model that calculates the size distribution of water-bearing planetesimals based on their adiabatic growth through the condensation of water vapor. 
Our model shows that these planetesimals can contain a significant amount of water, up to 80 percent by mass, within temperature ranges suitable for water condensation, which are 150 to 220 K. 
To verify this theoretical approach, we applied it to two specific planetesimals, Chelyabinsk and Benenitra, and found that they could have contained substantial amounts of water, which could have delivered a significant amount of water to early Earth. 
These findings suggest that the water found in chondrites can be explained by the hydrothermal planetesimal accumulation mechanism, which could have been a significant source of water for early Earth.

Using the quantum-group $U_q(\hat{gl}(N))$, we establish a general framework that extends the approach of Bazhanov, Baxter, and Reshetikhin to extend ZZ-eigenvalues for the XXZ spin chain to any desired depth, applicable to any matrix-size interaction within a specific range of the $\Delta$ parameter. This expansion reveals the underlying affine quantum-group symmetry present in the solvable XXZ model. We find the highest-weight states that define the irreducible representations and derive a recursive formula for the eigenvalues of the transfer matrix. This method yields the full set of transfer-matrix eigenvalues and their associated energies for both finite and infinite spin chains. Notably, our results hold true for both finite and infinite lengths of the spin chain.

This zero-shot voice interpretation approach enables a target language to be
achieved with minimal data, by training on a source language. We can transfer a
source language model to a target language that has no annotated data available.
Our method involves a single-step, source-to-target language translation, by
combining acoustic and translation models in a single end-to-end framework. A
single attention-based translator is trained, by learning to focus on corresponding
target and source speech. We show that the proposed method outperforms baseline
approaches, by using a single model rather than two separate models.

In the context of acoustic and electromagnetic wave interactions with spherical objects, the multipoles of scattering are significant. However, under the kR << 1 condition, inaccuracies arise in computing multipoles due to a singularity in the expansion of the wave number within the sphere. To circumvent this issue, a series transformation is proposed to calculate the scattering coefficients of higher multipoles independently of each other. This modified series, proposed, enables accurate evaluation of scattering and related quantities like acoustic or electromagnetic thrust, even when kR is not negligible.

This study introduces immanants of young tableaux and further develops the concept of quantum double young-capelli bitableaux. A revised connection between these bitableaux and the quantum Young symmetrizers is established, leading to the introduction of immanants of quantum Young symmetrizers. Additionally, connections to quantum Schur polynomials are found. The theory is expanded to encompass quantum double Schur polynomials, demonstrating a direct relationship. Altered Schur elements, introduced here, have a direct relationship with both classical and quantum Schur polynomials.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the possible dark matter behavior and model constraints resulting from laboratory experiments, cosmic observations, and influence on the stability of the electroweak vacuum. Utilizing a recently developed tool for dark matter parameter estimation, we examine the mass of the Standard Model's $W$ boson and dark matter within a specific range of new dark sector parameters that ensure the robustness of the Higgs vacuum. We find that a dark matter particle with a mass of approximately 10 GeV to 10 TeV is feasible and that a significant portion of the see-saw parameter space remains consistent with dark matter existence. We also determine that adding a non-standard interaction to the Standard Model may lead to vacuum decay, yet it is possible for it to exist in a long-lasting metastable state. We find that a significant portion of see-saw framework, including neutrally-tached dark matter, can be found. We also find that a dark matter candidate with a mass of approximately 10 GeV to 10 TeV is feasible and that a significant proportion of the see-saw parameter space remains consistent with dark matter existence.

The concept of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ orbital hybridization is explored for transition metals in various oxidation states from +1 to +7. Our analysis of experimental data from X-ray absorption spectroscopy and first-principles calculations reveals significant $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ hybridization in most compounds of Sc through Cu, with the exception of Cu$^{2+}$. Despite $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ being non-degenerate in an octahedral environment, we find that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ orbitals can overlap and hybridize when a crystal field splits the $e_g$ level. This level of orbital hybridization can actually exceed $t_{2g}$-$t_{2g}$ interactions.

Given a symplectic manifold M and a non-singular, rational map f from M to itself that has no critical points, we investigate the quantum homology of M. This research establishes the existence of a corresponding transformation F that also preserves the symplectic structure of M and M', such that the quantum homology of M' is fundamentally related to the quantum homology of M through the formula T_f^*H_*^{quant}(M') ~=~H_*^{quant}(M).

Our research team has developed a new approach to create a dataset for training deep learning models that can accurately predict the presence of diseases in chest X-rays. To achieve this, we designed an image modification technique that can mark specific regions in the X-rays and generate a dataset containing positive and negative examples. This innovative method is unique in its ability to correctly generate negative examples, a critical requirement for a balanced dataset. We tested our approach on three widely used public X-ray datasets and found that it produced high-quality images that deep learning models could use to achieve state-of-the-art results in disease prediction. Furthermore, our method is versatile and can be applied to any condition visible in X-rays, a capability that previous techniques lacked. These findings are visually supported by a series of graphical results.

ViDaExpert is an innovative software tool designed to facilitate non-linear visual exploration of multidimensional vector data. It integrates the principles of pair-wise and treemaps visualizations, facilitating an efficient examination of vast datasets. The software tool is user-friendly and user-customizable, facilitating the identification of vector data patterns and correlations. It is particularly useful in scenarios such as examining geopolitical data, financial data, and text embeddings.

We have developed a straightforward numerical method for rapidly computing Newtonian potentials and density distributions on planar regions. This method leverages Newton's identity to reduce the complexity of the integral from two to one dimension, significantly enhancing speed while maintaining accuracy. Common integration techniques can be applied to further improve precision with minimal computational overhead. When compared to existing methods, our approach offers comparable accuracy with much faster execution times, particularly for complex geometries and high-density points. We have demonstrated our technique through several test cases involving both simple and irregular two-dimensional areas.
